questions.stem: Solar energy reaches Earth as electromagnetic radiation. In which part of the spectrum is most of the Sun's energy emitted?
options: Long-wave infrared only
Visible light and nearby wavelengths
Radio waves and microwaves
X-rays and gamma rays
questions.explanation: The Sun's output peaks in the visible range, with large amounts of near-infrared and smaller amounts of ultraviolet. Earth, being much cooler, emits mainly long-wave infrared.

questions.stem: Which statement about ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun is correct?
options: It has shorter wavelengths and more energy per photon than visible light
It has longer wavelengths and less energy per photon than visible light
It has the same wavelength as infrared, but it travels much faster
It is emitted mainly by Earth's surface after it absorbs visible light
questions.explanation: UV lies beyond violet in the spectrum, so it has shorter wavelengths and higher energy per photon than visible light, which is why it can damage living cells. Infrared has longer wavelengths than visible light.

questions.stem: Most UV-C and much UV-B radiation from the Sun never reaches Earth's surface. Why?
options: It is reflected back to space by clouds in the troposphere
It is absorbed by water vapour near Earth's surface
It is bent around Earth by the magnetic field into space
It is absorbed by ozone and oxygen in the upper atmosphere
questions.explanation: Oxygen and ozone in the stratosphere and above absorb almost all UV-C and most UV-B, warming the stratosphere and shielding life. UV-A largely reaches the surface. Clouds reflect some sunlight but are not the main UV shield.

questions.stem: In studies of Earth's energy budget, the term albedo refers to:
options: The proportion of incoming solar radiation that a surface reflects
The proportion of infrared radiation absorbed by greenhouse gases
The amount of solar radiation reaching the top of the atmosphere
The rate at which a surface emits heat by conduction to the air
questions.explanation: Albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight a surface reflects, from 0 (none) to 1 (all). Light surfaces such as snow have high albedo; dark surfaces such as ocean and forest have low albedo.

questions.stem: Which surface would absorb the most solar energy on a sunny day?
options: Thick white cloud tops
Dark, open ocean water
Fresh snow on a mountain
Pale desert sand dunes
questions.explanation: Open ocean has a very low albedo, so it reflects little sunlight and absorbs most of it. Fresh snow and thick cloud reflect most incoming sunlight, and pale sand reflects more than dark water.

questions.stem: A city replaces dark bitumen car parks and roofs with light-coloured surfaces. What is the most likely effect on local temperatures, and why?
options: They rise, because higher albedo surfaces absorb more sunlight and emit more infrared
They rise, because light surfaces trap more greenhouse gases in the air above them
They fall, because light surfaces absorb more sunlight and store it underground
They fall, because higher albedo surfaces reflect more sunlight and absorb less energy
questions.explanation: Light surfaces have a higher albedo, so they reflect more incoming sunlight and absorb less, which reduces heating of the surface and the air above it. This principle is used in cool-roof and sustainable building design.

questions.stem: Tiny sulfate particles (aerosols) formed from gases in a large volcanic eruption spread through the stratosphere. What effect do they have on solar radiation reaching the surface?
options: They have no effect on sunlight, because they fall to the ground within hours
They reflect and scatter some sunlight back to space, so less reaches the surface
They absorb infrared from the surface and re-radiate it, so the surface warms
They destroy all ozone, so much more sunlight reaches the surface than before
questions.explanation: Sulfate aerosols reflect and back-scatter incoming sunlight, so less reaches the surface and global temperatures can dip for a year or two after a major eruption. Fine aerosols in the stable stratosphere remain aloft for many months rather than falling out in hours.

questions.stem: On average, about 30% of incoming solar radiation is reflected back to space by clouds, aerosols, air molecules and the surface. If 340 W/m² arrives at the top of the atmosphere, about how much is not reflected?
options: 238 W/m²
102 W/m²
310 W/m²
170 W/m²
questions.explanation: If 30% is reflected, 70% is absorbed by the atmosphere and surface: 0.70 × 340 = 238 W/m². The value 102 W/m² is the reflected part, not the part that remains.

questions.stem: Satellite data show Arctic sea ice shrinking in summer, exposing more open water. Why does this tend to increase warming in the region?
options: Open water blocks infrared from leaving, so no heat can escape from the ocean
Open water has a lower albedo than ice, so more sunlight is absorbed and more ice melts
Open water has a higher albedo than ice, so more sunlight is reflected and the air warms
Open water releases ozone, which absorbs extra infrared radiation above the region
questions.explanation: Ice reflects most sunlight, but dark open water absorbs most of it. Losing ice therefore increases energy absorption, which warms the water and melts more ice, a reinforcing (positive) feedback.

questions.stem: After Earth's surface absorbs solar radiation, it emits energy mainly as:
options: Ultraviolet radiation
Visible light
X-rays
Infrared radiation
questions.explanation: Earth's surface is far cooler than the Sun, so it emits energy at long wavelengths, as infrared radiation. Hot objects such as the Sun emit mostly visible and near-infrared light.

questions.stem: How do greenhouse gases warm Earth's surface?
options: They reflect incoming ultraviolet radiation back to the surface before it can escape to space
They form a solid layer that stops warm air from rising above the lower troposphere
They absorb infrared emitted by the surface and re-radiate it in all directions, including back down
They absorb incoming visible light from the Sun and convert it straight into heat in the air
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases are largely transparent to incoming visible light but absorb outgoing infrared. They then re-emit infrared in all directions, so some returns to the surface, which ends up warmer than it would be without them.

questions.stem: Which statement about the natural greenhouse effect is correct?
options: It cools Earth's surface by reflecting solar radiation back out to space
It occurs only on Venus and Mars, because Earth has too little carbon dioxide
It keeps Earth's average surface temperature well above freezing, allowing liquid water
It is caused only by human activities and did not exist before industrial times
questions.explanation: Naturally occurring water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane keep Earth's average surface temperature around 15 °C, rather than well below freezing. Human emissions enhance this natural effect; they did not create it.

questions.stem: Why do greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation but let most incoming sunlight through?
options: Sunlight comes from above and infrared from below, and gases absorb only from below
Their molecules absorb strongly at infrared wavelengths but weakly at visible wavelengths
Their molecules absorb strongly at visible wavelengths but weakly at infrared wavelengths
Incoming sunlight travels faster than infrared, so it passes before it can be absorbed
questions.explanation: Molecules such as CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O vibrate in ways that absorb particular infrared wavelengths, but they absorb little visible light. Since sunlight is mainly visible and Earth's emission is infrared, these gases act on outgoing energy. All EM radiation travels at the same speed.

questions.stem: Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's surface would radiate infrared straight to space. Which change would occur if greenhouse gas concentrations increased while solar input stayed constant?
options: More infrared escapes at first, so the surface cools until the gases are absorbed by the oceans
Solar input increases because greenhouse gases attract more sunlight towards Earth's surface
Nothing changes, because the extra gases re-radiate exactly as much energy into space as before
Less infrared escapes at first, so energy builds up until the surface warms enough to restore balance
questions.explanation: Extra greenhouse gases absorb more outgoing infrared, so for a time Earth emits less than it absorbs. By the first law, the extra energy is stored, warming the surface and lower atmosphere until emission rises to match input again.

questions.stem: Which gas makes the largest contribution to Earth's natural greenhouse effect?
options: Water vapour
Carbon dioxide
Methane
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Water vapour absorbs infrared over a wide range of wavelengths and is the largest contributor to the natural greenhouse effect. Nitrogen, the main gas in air, does not absorb infrared significantly.

questions.stem: Water vapour is the strongest greenhouse gas, yet human emissions of carbon dioxide are considered the main driver of recent warming. Why?
options: Human activities release more water vapour than carbon dioxide, but it cools the surface
Carbon dioxide absorbs visible light, while water vapour absorbs only ultraviolet radiation
Water vapour levels mainly respond to temperature, while added CO₂ persists and sets the temperature
Water vapour is not a greenhouse gas at all, so it has no effect on the temperature of Earth
questions.explanation: Excess water vapour rains out within days, so its concentration is controlled by temperature. Carbon dioxide remains in the atmosphere for a long time, so increases in CO₂ raise temperatures, which then increase water vapour, amplifying the warming as a feedback.

questions.stem: Which is a major source of atmospheric methane?
options: Evaporation from the oceans
Digestion in cattle and sheep
Photosynthesis in rainforests
Weathering of granite rocks
questions.explanation: Microbes in the guts of ruminant livestock produce methane, which the animals release. Other sources include wetlands, rice paddies, landfill and leaks from fossil fuel extraction. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide and does not release methane.

questions.stem: Which list gives sources of carbon dioxide only?
options: Burning fossil fuels, clearing and burning forests, and making cement
Livestock digestion, rice paddies and decomposition in landfill
Refrigerants in old fridges, aerosol sprays and air conditioners
Evaporation from oceans, transpiration and boiling water in kettles
questions.explanation: Combustion of coal, oil and gas, burning of cleared vegetation and the chemical reaction in cement production all release CO₂. Livestock, rice paddies and landfill are methane sources, CFCs come from refrigerants and sprays, and evaporation adds water vapour.

questions.stem: Methane traps much more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide but stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade. What does this mean for reducing emissions?
options: Cutting methane has no benefit, because it disappears from the air within a few days anyway
Cutting CO₂ gives a fast reduction in warming, because it is removed in about ten years
Cutting either gas has the same effect over every timescale, because both are greenhouse gases
Cutting methane gives a fast reduction in warming, while cutting CO₂ matters for the long term
questions.explanation: Because methane is potent but short-lived, reducing methane emissions lowers warming within decades. Added CO₂ persists for centuries, so its reductions determine long-term warming. Both matter, but on different timescales.

questions.stem: Air in bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice shows CO₂ at about 280 ppm before industrialisation, and modern direct measurements show much higher values. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Ice cores record water vapour, not CO₂, so no conclusion can be drawn
CO₂ levels have fallen since industrialisation as forests have expanded
Human activities since industrialisation have greatly increased atmospheric CO₂
Natural CO₂ levels have always been higher than today, so the change is normal
questions.explanation: Pre-industrial levels of about 280 ppm, compared with much higher modern values, show a large rise that coincides with fossil fuel burning and land clearing. Ice-core bubbles preserve samples of ancient air, including its CO₂.

questions.stem: Students place thermometers in two identical sealed jars under the same lamp. Jar A contains air and jar B contains air with extra carbon dioxide. Which variable must be controlled to make the comparison valid?
options: The difference in temperature between jars
The distance from the lamp to each jar
The amount of carbon dioxide in each jar
The final temperature of each jar
questions.explanation: To test the effect of carbon dioxide (the independent variable), everything else, such as lamp distance, jar size and starting temperature, must be the same. The temperature is the dependent variable that is measured.

questions.stem: In the jar experiment, both jars warm well above room temperature, and the jar with extra CO₂ warms a little more. Which statement best evaluates this model?
options: The extra warming proves that CO₂ absorbs visible light rather than infrared radiation
The model is invalid, because carbon dioxide has no effect on the temperature of air
Much of the warming in both jars comes from trapped air not mixing, unlike the open atmosphere
The model shows perfectly how the atmosphere warms, so no limitations need to be considered
questions.explanation: A sealed jar warms partly because the lid stops warm air escaping by convection, which is not how the atmosphere works. The small extra warming with CO₂ is consistent with infrared absorption, but the model exaggerates and simplifies the real greenhouse effect.

questions.stem: Venus is further from the Sun than Mercury, yet Venus has the higher average surface temperature. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Venus has no atmosphere at all, so all of its sunlight reaches and heats the surface
Venus has a very thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide that produces an extreme greenhouse effect
Venus has a much higher albedo than Mercury, so it absorbs far more of the sunlight it receives
Venus has an active core that produces more heat than the Sun supplies to Mercury
questions.explanation: Venus's dense atmosphere, about 96% carbon dioxide, traps outgoing infrared so effectively that its surface is hotter than Mercury's. Venus's bright clouds actually give it a high albedo, so it reflects much of the sunlight it receives.

questions.stem: Mars's atmosphere is about 95% carbon dioxide, a higher percentage than Earth's, yet Mars has only a small greenhouse effect. What best explains this?
options: Mars's atmosphere is extremely thin, so the total amount of greenhouse gas is small
Carbon dioxide on Mars absorbs visible light instead of infrared radiation
Mars is closer to the Sun than Earth, so it does not need a greenhouse effect
Mars has more water vapour than Earth, which cancels out the effect of CO₂
questions.explanation: The strength of the greenhouse effect depends on the total amount of greenhouse gas, not just its percentage. Mars's surface pressure is less than 1% of Earth's, so there is little gas to absorb infrared. Mars is further from the Sun than Earth.

questions.stem: A graph shows global average temperature and atmospheric CO₂ since 1900, both rising, with temperature showing more year-to-year variation. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Temperature rises cause CO₂ to rise, so burning fuels has no effect on the climate
The two variables are unrelated, because their graphs do not have identical shapes
The long-term rise matches the rise in CO₂, with natural year-to-year variability on top
The year-to-year variation proves that CO₂ has no effect on global average temperature
questions.explanation: Long-term trends are compared, not single years. Natural factors such as El Niño and volcanic eruptions cause year-to-year variation around a rising trend that matches the increase in CO₂. Physical understanding of infrared absorption supports a causal link.

questions.stem: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were widely used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays because they are non-toxic and unreactive near the ground. Which unintended consequences were later discovered?
options: They react with nitrogen to make the air poisonous for animals
They destroy stratospheric ozone and are also potent greenhouse gases
They form acid rain and make the soils in forests very alkaline
They block sunlight in the troposphere and cool the surface greatly
questions.explanation: CFCs drift to the stratosphere, where UV breaks them down and releases chlorine that destroys ozone. They also absorb infrared strongly, so they add to the greenhouse effect. These discoveries led to their phase-out.

questions.stem: Which international agreement, signed in 1987, phased out the production of CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances?
options: The Kyoto Protocol
The Paris Agreement
The Antarctic Treaty
The Montreal Protocol
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol controls ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs. The Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement deal with greenhouse gas emissions, and the Antarctic Treaty governs the use of Antarctica.

questions.stem: Some replacements for CFCs, such as certain hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), do not harm the ozone layer. Why are they still a concern?
options: They are poisonous to people at the concentrations found in the air
They absorb visible sunlight, which makes the sky noticeably darker
Many are strong greenhouse gases, so they add to global warming
They destroy ozone even faster than CFCs once in the stratosphere
questions.explanation: HFCs contain no chlorine, so they do not destroy ozone, but many absorb infrared strongly and have high global warming potentials. Solving one environmental problem created a contribution to another, an example of unintended consequences.

questions.stem: A house in Brisbane is designed with large north-facing windows and wide eaves. How does this use knowledge of solar energy?
options: Eaves block all winter sun and let summer sun in, so the house is warmer in summer
North-facing windows receive no direct sunlight in the Southern Hemisphere at any time
Eaves reflect infrared from inside the house back out, keeping it cool in winter
Eaves shade the high summer sun but let the low winter sun shine in to warm the house
questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere the Sun is in the northern sky. In summer it is high, so eaves shade the windows; in winter it is low, so sunlight passes under the eaves and warms the house. This passive solar design reduces energy use.

questions.stem: A solar photovoltaic panel converts:
options: Electrical energy into light energy
Infrared energy into kinetic energy
Light energy into electrical energy
Heat energy into chemical energy
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic cells convert light energy directly into electrical energy. Solar hot water systems, by contrast, use solar energy to heat water.

questions.stem: Earth's average surface temperature is about 15 °C. Models of a planet at Earth's distance from the Sun with no greenhouse gases give about −18 °C. What is the warming caused by the natural greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation: The warming is the difference between the actual and modelled temperatures: 15 − (−18) = 33 °C. Subtracting 15 − 18 instead gives −3, a sign error.

questions.stem: Why do clouds both cool and warm Earth's surface?
options: They absorb incoming sunlight, but they also reflect outgoing ultraviolet radiation
They produce oxygen by day, which cools the air, and methane at night, which warms it
They reflect infrared from space and absorb visible light from the surface
They reflect incoming sunlight, but they also absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared
questions.explanation: Cloud tops have a high albedo, reflecting sunlight and cooling the surface by day. Clouds also absorb infrared from the surface and re-radiate some back down, which is why cloudy nights stay warmer than clear nights.

questions.stem: On a clear, still winter night in Toowoomba, the temperature falls much lower than on a cloudy night. What best explains the difference?
options: Clouds absorb heat from the ground and keep it, so cloudy nights cool the ground faster
Clear skies contain more carbon dioxide, which absorbs heat from the ground and cools it
Without cloud, more infrared from the ground escapes to space, so the surface cools more
Without cloud, more sunlight reaches the ground at night, so the air cools more quickly
questions.explanation: On clear nights, infrared emitted by the ground passes more easily to space, so temperatures drop sharply and frost can form. Clouds absorb that infrared and re-radiate some back down, keeping the surface warmer. No sunlight arrives at night.

questions.stem: Which of these atmospheric gases is not a significant greenhouse gas?
options: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
Oxygen (O₂)
Methane (CH₄)
Water vapour (H₂O)
questions.explanation: Oxygen and nitrogen, made of two identical atoms, absorb very little infrared, so they are not significant greenhouse gases even though they make up most of the air. Methane, water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb infrared strongly.

questions.stem: A new office building is designed to be carbon neutral. Which combination of features best uses knowledge of solar energy to achieve this?
options: Black external walls, single glazing and gas heaters running throughout the year
Rooftop solar panels, shading of summer sun, high-albedo roofing and good insulation
Dark roofing to absorb sunlight, large west-facing glass walls and diesel generators
No windows at all, constant air conditioning and electricity from a coal-fired station
questions.explanation: Generating electricity from sunlight, shading summer sun, reflecting sunlight with light roofs and insulating to reduce heating and cooling all lower energy use and emissions. Dark surfaces and large west-facing glass increase heat gain in a Queensland summer.

questions.stem: Ultraviolet radiation reaching the surface is greater in Queensland in summer than in winter. Which factor mainly explains this?
options: The ozone layer is thicker in summer, so it emits more ultraviolet radiation
Earth is much further from the Sun in summer, so the radiation is stronger
Summer clouds produce ultraviolet radiation when they reflect visible light
The Sun is higher in the sky, so its rays pass through less atmosphere and ozone
questions.explanation: When the Sun is high, its rays take a shorter path through the atmosphere, so less UV is absorbed by ozone before reaching the ground. Ozone absorbs UV rather than emitting it, and Earth's distance from the Sun changes only slightly through the year.
